prompt: If the Federal Reserve conducts open-market purchases of Treasuries, the most likely near-term effect is

options.text: Reduced bank reserves and upward pressure on short-term interest rates
Higher reserve requirements that restrict new bank lending
An immediate cut in federal income tax rates by Congress
Increased bank reserves and downward pressure on short-term rates

explanation: When the Fed buys Treasuries, it pays the sellers by crediting bank reserve accounts. Those extra reserves reduce banks' need to borrow overnight, so the federal funds rate tends to fall in the near term.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses open-market purchases with open-market sales; sales drain reserves and push short-term rates up.
distractorExplanations.b: Reserve requirements are a separate Fed tool; buying Treasuries changes reserve balances, not the required ratio.
distractorExplanations.c: Tax-rate cuts are fiscal policy enacted by Congress, not a result of Federal Reserve open-market operations.

prompt: Mr. Chen is in the 32% federal bracket and pays no state income tax. A municipal bond yields 3.40%. What yield would a taxable corporate bond need to match it after tax?

options.text: 2.31 percent
4.49 percent
5.00 percent
10.63 percent

explanation: Tax-equivalent yield = muni yield ÷ (1 − marginal rate) = 3.40% ÷ (1 − 0.32) = 3.40% ÷ 0.68 = 5.00%. A taxable bond yielding 5.00% keeps 5.00% × 0.68 = 3.40% after federal tax, matching the muni.

distractorExplanations.a: Multiplies by 0.68, which gives the after-tax yield of a taxable 3.40% bond, not the taxable yield needed to equal the muni.
distractorExplanations.b: Multiplies by 1.32 instead of dividing by 0.68; grossing up by the tax rate understates the required taxable yield.
distractorExplanations.d: Divides by the 32% tax rate instead of by one minus the rate, more than doubling the true tax-equivalent yield.

Moved about 20% more than the market on average
Returned 1.2% more than the market each year
Had 20% total volatility (standard deviation)

The extra cost of producing one more unit
The value of the next-best alternative forgone

prompt: When aggregate demand rises faster than aggregate supply, inflationary pressure is most likely to

options.text: Disappear because markets self-correct overnight
Fall because producers cut prices voluntarily
Remain unchanged regardless of demand
Increase as prices are bid up across the economy

explanation: When aggregate demand outruns what firms can produce, buyers compete for the same goods. That competition bids prices up across many markets, which is how excess demand becomes inflationary pressure.

distractorExplanations.a: Assumes excess demand vanishes overnight; buyers can bid prices up before supply catches up, so the inflation pressure does not disappear at once.
distractorExplanations.b: Reverses the price response; when demand outruns supply, producers tend to raise prices rather than cut them voluntarily.
distractorExplanations.c: Treats the price level as independent of demand; a rise in aggregate demand relative to supply is what bids the general price level higher.

prompt: The unemployment rate measures the percentage of the labor force that is

options.text: Without a job and actively seeking work
Retired and no longer counted in population
Working part-time by choice
Employed but dissatisfied with wages

explanation: The unemployment rate divides people without a job who searched recently by the labor force. Someone who is not looking, including a retiree, is outside that ratio and is not counted as unemployed.

distractorExplanations.b: Retirees are outside the labor force, and the unemployment rate is a share of the labor force, so retirees are left out of that percentage.
distractorExplanations.c: Someone working part-time by choice already has a job, so that person is employed and is not counted in the unemployment rate.
distractorExplanations.d: Workers who have a job but dislike the pay are employed; dissatisfaction with wages does not put them in the unemployed count.

prompt: The Federal Reserve's statutory dual mandate seeks

options.text: Zero federal budget deficits every year
Maximum employment and stable prices
Fixed exchange rates with all trading partners
Guaranteed positive stock returns

explanation: Congress gave the Fed a dual mandate of maximum employment and stable prices, and the Fed pursues those goals with monetary tools. The mandate does not assign the Fed the federal budget or a fixed exchange rate.

distractorExplanations.a: A zero budget deficit is a fiscal result for Congress and the Treasury, not one of the Fed's statutory goals for employment and prices.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses the dual mandate with an exchange-rate peg; the Fed is charged with employment and stable prices, and the dollar floats.
distractorExplanations.d: The mandate does not promise investors a gain in stocks; share prices can fall even when employment and inflation goals are met.

prompt: Deflation, as distinguished from a one-time price dip, is best described as

options.text: Rising wages across all sectors simultaneously
A one-day drop in gasoline prices
A sustained decline in the general price level
Higher nominal GDP in current dollars

explanation: Deflation is a continuing drop in the broad price level, so many prices are falling over time. A one-day dip in a single product is not deflation, and neither is disinflation, which is a slower but still positive inflation rate.

distractorExplanations.a: A broad rise in wages is a labor-cost change, not the sustained fall in the general price level that defines deflation.
distractorExplanations.b: A one-day drop in gasoline is a single-product move; deflation requires a sustained decline in the overall price level.
distractorExplanations.d: Higher nominal GDP counts current-dollar output and can rise while prices rise, so it does not describe deflation.

prompt: A recession, in the sense used for U.S. business-cycle dating, is commonly defined as

options.text: A single quarter of negative real GDP growth
A 20% decline in a broad stock market index from its peak
A sustained rise in the general price level across the economy
A significant decline in economic activity spread across the economy

explanation: U.S. business-cycle dating treats a recession as a significant decline in activity that is spread across the economy and lasts more than a few months, judged from output, income, and jobs together. One weak quarter or a 20% stock drop is a different test.

distractorExplanations.a: One weak quarter is not enough; recessions involve broad, sustained declines across the economy.
distractorExplanations.b: A 20% index decline from the peak is the common bear market definition, not a recession.
distractorExplanations.c: A sustained rise in the general price level is inflation, not a decline in economic activity.

prompt: If the Fed sells Treasury securities in open-market operations, bank reserves will most likely

options.text: Decrease, tightening monetary conditions
Increase because cash leaves the banking system
Stay fixed because OMOs are symbolic
Rise because the Fed pays interest on excess reserves

explanation: When the Fed sells Treasury securities, buyers pay with bank reserves, so reserve balances fall and short-term credit conditions tighten.

distractorExplanations.b: Reverses the reserve effect; open-market sales drain reserves, while open-market purchases are the operations that add reserves.
distractorExplanations.c: Treats open-market sales as symbolic; a sale actually removes reserve balances from the banking system.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses interest on reserve balances, a separate administered rate, with the reserve drain caused by selling securities.

prompt: The Phillips curve concept describes a short-run relationship between

options.text: Stock beta and bond duration
Inflation and unemployment
Corporate dividends and share buybacks
Trade deficits and currency pegs

explanation: Historically, lower unemployment has sometimes coincided with higher inflation in the short run. That pattern is a short-run tradeoff, not a rule that the two always move together.

distractorExplanations.a: Beta and duration measure a security's market sensitivity and rate sensitivity; the Phillips curve links inflation with unemployment.
distractorExplanations.c: Dividend and buyback choices are corporate payout policy, not the short-run macro link between inflation and unemployment.
distractorExplanations.d: Trade deficits and currency pegs belong to international finance; they are not the Phillips curve's inflation-unemployment relationship.

prompt: An unexpected rise in consumer confidence typically supports

options.text: Lower consumer spending as households save more
Immediate Fed rate cuts to support demand
Higher consumer spending and near-term growth
Lower bond yields as investors seek safety

explanation: A rise in consumer confidence usually leads households to spend a larger share of income, which lifts near-term aggregate demand and growth.

distractorExplanations.a: Rising confidence usually lowers precautionary saving and raises spending, not the reverse.
distractorExplanations.b: Stronger confidence boosts demand on its own; it does not call for Fed rate cuts to support demand.
distractorExplanations.d: Optimism tends to push yields up as investors move away from safe assets, not toward them.

prompt: A sharp increase in oil prices is an example of a

options.text: Demand-side stimulus from lower energy bills
Demand-pull inflation driven by excess spending
Monetary policy tightening by the Federal Reserve
Supply-side shock that can raise production costs

explanation: Oil is an input for transport and production in many industries. A sharp price increase raises those costs even when household demand has not risen, so the shock comes from supply rather than from a spending boom or a Fed action.

distractorExplanations.a: Treats an oil-price spike as a cut in household energy bills; higher oil prices raise production costs rather than stimulating demand.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses cost-push with demand-pull; an oil price spike raises costs from the supply side.
distractorExplanations.c: Oil prices are set in commodity markets; Fed tightening is a policy action, not a supply shock.

prompt: In the equation of exchange, the velocity of money refers to

options.text: How frequently money changes hands in the economy
The rate at which the Fed expands the money supply
The share of income households save each year
How quickly bank deposits multiply through lending

explanation: In the equation of exchange, MV = PY, velocity is how many times the money stock is spent on final goods during the period. It is the turnover of existing money, not the rate at which the Fed grows the money supply.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses velocity with the growth of the money supply; in MV = PY, a change in M is how fast the stock grows, while V is how often each dollar is spent.
distractorExplanations.c: The share of income saved is the personal saving rate, not the velocity of money.
distractorExplanations.d: Deposit expansion through lending is the money multiplier, a different concept from velocity.

prompt: All else equal, a stronger U.S. dollar tends to

options.text: Make U.S. exports more competitive abroad
Make imported goods cheaper for U.S. buyers
Raise the dollar value of foreign investment returns
Make foreign travel more expensive for Americans

explanation: Each dollar converts into more foreign currency, so a given foreign price costs fewer dollars. Imported goods therefore become cheaper for U.S. buyers, while U.S. goods become more expensive for foreign buyers.

distractorExplanations.a: Reverses the export effect; a stronger dollar makes U.S. goods more expensive abroad, so exports become less competitive, not more.
distractorExplanations.c: A stronger dollar reduces the dollar value of foreign-currency returns for U.S. investors.
distractorExplanations.d: A stronger dollar buys more foreign currency, making foreign travel cheaper for Americans.

prompt: Crowding out in fiscal policy occurs when

options.text: Higher tax revenue pushes down interest rates and increases private business investment
Government spending raises private incomes and multiplies total output
Higher government borrowing pushes up interest rates and reduces private investment
Fed bond purchases push down interest rates and boost private borrowing

explanation: Deficit financing adds Treasury demand for loanable funds. That extra demand can push market interest rates up, and the higher rates can reduce the private investment that would have been financed at the old rate.

distractorExplanations.a: That describes crowding in from reduced government borrowing, the opposite of crowding out.
distractorExplanations.b: That is the fiscal multiplier effect, not the rate-driven reduction in private investment.
distractorExplanations.d: That describes monetary easing such as quantitative easing, not fiscal crowding out.

prompt: The natural rate of unemployment includes

options.text: Frictional and cyclical unemployment at full employment
Cyclical unemployment caused by recession layoffs
Workers who have stopped looking for work
Frictional and structural unemployment at full employment

explanation: The natural rate is the unemployment left at full employment: people between jobs (frictional) and people whose skills no longer match openings (structural). Recession layoffs, which are cyclical, are treated as zero at that rate.

distractorExplanations.a: Cyclical unemployment is near zero at the natural rate; it is frictional plus structural.
distractorExplanations.b: Recession layoffs are cyclical unemployment, which is excluded from the natural rate.
distractorExplanations.c: Discouraged workers are outside the labor force and are not counted in the unemployment rate.

prompt: Reserve requirements have been 0% since March 2020. If the Fed raised them again, member banks would have to:

options.text: Hold a larger fraction of deposits as reserves, reducing funds available to lend
Hold a smaller fraction of deposits as reserves, increasing funds available to lend
Raise the discount rate charged on overnight borrowing from the Fed
Hold more capital against loans under Basel risk-weighting standards

explanation: The Fed cut reserve requirement ratios to 0% in March 2020, but in principle raising them forces banks to hold a larger share of deposits as reserves, shrinking excess reserves and the money multiplier and reducing lending capacity.

distractorExplanations.b: Reverses the effect; a higher requirement ties up more deposits and reduces lending capacity.
distractorExplanations.c: The Fed sets the discount rate; member banks do not raise it in response to reserve requirements.
distractorExplanations.d: Capital requirements are a separate bank regulation; reserve requirements apply to deposits.

prompt: During an aggressive Fed tightening cycle, a yield curve that flattens may indicate

options.text: Long rates must exceed short rates by a fixed statutory margin
Markets expect slower growth or eventual rate cuts further out
Inflation expectations have fallen to zero permanently
The Treasury will stop issuing new bonds

explanation: Flattening can signal expectations that policy will constrain growth or that long rates will fall relative to short rates.

distractorExplanations.a: Invents a statutory gap between long and short yields; no statute requires long rates to exceed short rates by a fixed margin.
distractorExplanations.c: Reads one flattening as proof that inflation expectations are stuck at zero forever, which the curve shape does not establish.
distractorExplanations.d: Ties the curve's shape to a halt in Treasury issuance; the Treasury keeps auctioning debt whether or not the curve flattens.

prompt: Nominal GDP grew 6% last year while the GDP price deflator rose 4%. Approximate real GDP growth for that year was

options.text: 2 percent
4 percent
6 percent
10 percent

explanation: Approximate real GDP growth equals nominal GDP growth minus inflation from the price deflator. Subtracting the 4% price rise from 6% nominal growth leaves about 2% growth in real output.

distractorExplanations.b: Uses the 4% deflator by itself and never subtracts it from the 6% nominal growth, so it reports inflation rather than real output growth.
distractorExplanations.c: Reports the 6% nominal GDP growth and leaves the 4% price increase inside the figure, so prices are still mixed into the growth rate.
distractorExplanations.d: Adds the 6% nominal growth to the 4% deflator instead of subtracting, which counts inflation twice and overstates real growth.

prompt: A one-year Treasury yields a nominal 7.0%, and expected inflation over that year is 3.0%. The approximate real rate is

options.text: 4.0 percent
7.0 percent
10.0 percent
21.0 percent

explanation: The Fisher approximation sets the real rate equal to the nominal yield minus expected inflation. Here 7.0% minus 3.0% is 4.0%, the inflation-adjusted return before compounding.

distractorExplanations.b: Stops at the 7.0% nominal Treasury yield and never subtracts the 3.0% inflation that reduces the investor's purchasing power.
distractorExplanations.c: Adds the 7.0% yield to 3.0% expected inflation, which grosses up the real rate instead of removing the price change.
distractorExplanations.d: Multiplies 7 by 3 and treats the two percentages as factors, rather than subtracting inflation from the nominal yield.

prompt: A firm reports current assets of $240,000 and current liabilities of $150,000. Its working capital is
explanation: Working capital is current assets minus current liabilities. Subtracting $150,000 of current liabilities from $240,000 of current assets leaves $90,000 of net current resources.

distractorExplanations.b: Reports current liabilities alone and never subtracts them from current assets, so it is not the net working-capital balance.
distractorExplanations.c: Reports current assets alone and skips the subtraction of current liabilities that the working-capital formula requires.
distractorExplanations.d: Adds current assets to current liabilities. Working capital is the difference between those balances, not their sum.

prompt: A company has total assets of $1,000,000 and total liabilities of $400,000. Its debt-to-assets ratio is

options.text: 40 percent
60 percent
150 percent
250 percent

explanation: The debt-to-assets ratio divides total liabilities by total assets. Here $400,000 divided by $1,000,000 equals 0.40, so debt finances 40% of assets.

distractorExplanations.b: Divides equity of $600,000 by assets, which is the equity ratio, not the share of assets financed by liabilities.
distractorExplanations.c: Divides equity of $600,000 by liabilities of $400,000, an equity-to-debt figure of 1.5, instead of liabilities over assets.
distractorExplanations.d: Inverts the ratio by dividing total assets by total liabilities, which produces 2.5 rather than the 0.40 debt-to-assets ratio.

prompt: A client will receive $10,000 in two years. Discounted at an annual rate of 5%, the present value is closest to
explanation: Present value discounts the future amount once for each year it is delayed. At 5% for two years, $10,000 divided by 1.05 squared, or 1.1025, is about $9,070.

distractorExplanations.b: Discounts for only one year at 5%, using $10,000 divided by 1.05, and leaves out the second year of discounting.
distractorExplanations.c: Leaves the $10,000 undiscounted, which ignores the 5% time value of waiting two years to receive the cash.
distractorExplanations.d: Compounds $10,000 forward at 5% for two years, which is a future value, not the present value of a sum received later.

prompt: Which measure most often moves at the same time as current economic activity, rather than before or after it?

options.text: Nonfarm payroll employment
Building permits for new private housing
The average number of weeks people remain unemployed
Prices in a broad index of common stocks

explanation: Nonfarm payroll employment rises and falls with the current pace of hiring, so it is a coincident indicator of activity already underway.

distractorExplanations.b: Housing permits are issued before construction spending shows up in output, so they lead the cycle instead of moving with it.
distractorExplanations.c: The average length of unemployment keeps rising after a downturn has started, which makes it a lagging indicator.
distractorExplanations.d: Broad stock prices usually turn before GDP does, so they are watched as a leading indicator rather than a coincident one.

prompt: During the contraction phase of the business cycle, which pattern is most typical?

options.text: Real output falls and the unemployment rate rises
Real output rises and the unemployment rate falls
Real output rises while firms draw down inventories
Unemployment falls as discouraged workers leave the labor force

explanation: A contraction is the declining phase of the cycle. Real GDP and production fall, and the unemployment rate typically rises as firms cut hours and jobs.

distractorExplanations.b: Describes an expansion, when output is rising and unemployment is falling, which is the opposite of a contraction.
distractorExplanations.c: Rising output with falling inventories is an expansion that is using up stock, not a phase in which production is declining.
distractorExplanations.d: Exits from the labor force can hide some joblessness, but a typical contraction still shows a rising unemployment rate, not a falling one.

prompt: Real GDP has fallen for three quarters. The decline then stops and factories start recalling laid-off workers. Cycle dating calls that turning point a

options.text: Trough, because the contraction is ending and recovery is starting
Peak, because the expansion is ending and a downturn is starting
Plateau, because prices and output have stopped changing for good
Full-employment point, because the jobless rate has reached zero

explanation: The trough is the bottom of a contraction. When a three-quarter decline in real GDP ends and firms begin recalling workers, the contraction is over and the recovery is starting.

distractorExplanations.b: A peak ends an expansion. This episode ends a three-quarter decline in real GDP, so the turning point is a trough, not a peak.
distractorExplanations.c: A trough is a turn back toward growth, not a permanent stop in both prices and output. The stem says factories are recalling workers.
distractorExplanations.d: Recalling some laid-off workers does not mean the unemployment rate is zero. A trough can occur with many people still out of work.

prompt: Which statement correctly describes the federal funds rate used in monetary policy?

options.text: The overnight rate on loans of reserves between banks
The rate the Fed charges on discount-window loans
The auction yield on new 10-year Treasury notes
The rate banks advertise to their strongest borrowers

explanation: The federal funds rate is the market rate on overnight loans of reserve balances from one bank to another. The Fed sets a target for it and steers that target with its policy tools.

distractorExplanations.b: Describes the discount rate, which is what banks pay to borrow from the Federal Reserve, not the overnight rate banks charge one another.
distractorExplanations.c: The Treasury's auction yield on the 10-year note is a long-term market yield, not the overnight interbank federal funds rate.
distractorExplanations.d: Describes the prime rate, a benchmark banks quote to creditworthy customers, which is not the overnight rate on reserve loans.

prompt: A savings account pays a nominal 3% while inflation is running at 5%. The approximate real rate on the account is

options.text: Negative 2 percent
Positive 2 percent
Positive 3 percent
Positive 8 percent

explanation: The approximate real rate equals the nominal rate minus inflation. A 3% nominal rate minus 5% inflation is about negative 2%, so the deposit loses purchasing power.

distractorExplanations.b: Subtracts in the wrong order, 5% minus 3%, and reports a gain. Inflation is above the nominal rate, so the real rate is negative.
distractorExplanations.c: Reports the 3% nominal rate and ignores the 5% inflation that has to be subtracted to reach the real rate.
distractorExplanations.d: Adds the 3% nominal rate to 5% inflation and gets 8%, treating the price rise as extra yield instead of a subtraction.

prompt: Cash is $50,000, receivables are $70,000, inventory is $80,000, and current liabilities are $100,000. The quick ratio is
explanation: The quick ratio divides the most liquid current assets, cash plus receivables, by current liabilities and leaves inventory out. ($50,000 + $70,000) / $100,000 = 1.20.

distractorExplanations.a: Divides only the $50,000 cash balance by current liabilities and leaves out the $70,000 of receivables that the quick ratio includes.
distractorExplanations.c: Adds the $80,000 of inventory to cash and drops receivables. Inventory is the asset the quick ratio excludes, while receivables stay in.
distractorExplanations.d: Divides all $200,000 of current assets by current liabilities. That is the current ratio, because inventory is still included.

prompt: A stock trades at $48 and the company just reported earnings of $3.00 per share. The price-to-earnings ratio is

options.text: 3 times
16 times
45 times
51 times

explanation: The price-to-earnings ratio divides the market price by earnings per share. Dividing $48 by $3.00 gives 16, so the stock trades at 16 times those earnings.

distractorExplanations.a: Stops at the $3.00 earnings-per-share figure and never divides the $48 market price by that earnings number.
distractorExplanations.c: Subtracts the $3.00 of earnings from the $48 price, a dollar difference, instead of dividing price by earnings per share.
distractorExplanations.d: Adds the $3.00 of earnings to the $48 price, which is not the ratio of price divided by earnings per share.

prompt: Nominal GDP is $15.0 trillion and the GDP price deflator is 125 on a base of 100. Real GDP is closest to

options.text: $10.0 trillion
$12.0 trillion
$15.0 trillion
$18.75 trillion

explanation: Real GDP removes the price level by dividing nominal GDP by the deflator stated relative to 100. $15.0 trillion divided by 1.25 equals $12.0 trillion in base-year prices.

distractorExplanations.a: Divides by 1.50, as if the deflator were 150 rather than 125, and that mistake understates real output at $10.0 trillion.
distractorExplanations.c: Reports the $15.0 trillion nominal GDP and never divides by 1.25, so the figure still includes the higher price level.
distractorExplanations.d: Multiplies $15.0 trillion by 1.25, which inflates nominal GDP a second time instead of deflating it to real output.

prompt: Which measure most often turns only after the business cycle has already changed direction?

options.text: Weekly initial claims for unemployment insurance
The average number of weeks people remain unemployed
Manufacturers' new orders for consumer goods
A broad index of common-stock prices

explanation: The average duration of unemployment keeps lengthening after a recession has started and shortens only after hiring recovers, so it lags the cycle.

distractorExplanations.a: Initial jobless claims change before the broad economy turns, so they are a leading indicator rather than a lagging one.
distractorExplanations.c: New orders are placed before the related production is recorded, so they lead economic activity instead of lagging it.
distractorExplanations.d: A broad stock index usually moves ahead of GDP, which is why equity prices are treated as a leading indicator.

prompt: Factory output and household spending rose for two years. This quarter both stall, and new orders turn down. Where is the business cycle?

options.text: At a trough, because the long decline is ending
At a peak, because the expansion is giving way to contraction
In deflation, because consumer prices fell for two years
At full employment, because the jobless rate is zero

explanation: The peak is the high point of an expansion. When output and spending stop rising and new orders turn down, the expansion is ending and a contraction is beginning.

distractorExplanations.a: A trough is the end of a decline, not the end of a two-year rise in output and spending. This stall after an expansion is a peak.
distractorExplanations.c: Deflation would be a sustained fall in the price level. The facts given are a high in real activity and weaker orders, not two years of falling prices.
distractorExplanations.d: Full employment is not an unemployment rate of zero, and a peak can occur while some workers are still without jobs.

prompt: Congress cuts the corporate tax rate from 21% to 18% and raises infrastructure outlays. This package is best classified as

options.text: Contractionary monetary policy run by the Federal Reserve
Expansionary fiscal policy run by the federal government
An increase in the discount rate charged by the Federal Reserve
An open-market sale of Treasury securities by the Federal Reserve

explanation: Cutting taxes and raising government spending are fiscal tools. Moving the corporate rate from 21% to 18% and adding outlays increases demand, so the package is expansionary fiscal policy.

distractorExplanations.a: Assigns a congressional tax-and-spending change to the Fed. Monetary policy works through rates and reserves, not the corporate tax rate.
distractorExplanations.c: A higher discount rate is a Federal Reserve tightening step. It is not a tax cut from 21% to 18% paired with new public spending.
distractorExplanations.d: An open-market sale drains bank reserves and tightens money. It is not a congressional cut in the corporate tax rate.

prompt: An investor deposits $10,000 for two years at a 5% annual compound rate and adds nothing further. The future value is closest to
explanation: Compound future value applies the rate to the growing balance. $10,000 times 1.05 squared equals $10,000 times 1.1025, which is $11,025.

distractorExplanations.a: Credits only one year of 5% interest, or $500, and omits the second year in which that interest also earns interest.
distractorExplanations.b: Uses simple interest of $500 a year for two years and skips the extra $25 earned by compounding the first year's interest.
distractorExplanations.d: Applies a flat 20% to the deposit, as if two years at 5% were 20%, and that overstates two years of 5% compound growth.

prompt: Using the rule of 72, about how many years does it take an investment to double at an annual compound rate of 8%?

options.text: 6 years
8 years
9 years
12 years

explanation: The rule of 72 estimates doubling time by dividing 72 by the annual interest rate in percent. At 8%, 72 divided by 8 equals 9 years.

distractorExplanations.a: Divides 72 by 12 rather than by the 8% rate, which is the doubling-time estimate for a 12% rate, not for 8%.
distractorExplanations.b: Treats the 8% rate itself as the number of years and never divides 72 by that rate.
distractorExplanations.d: Divides 72 by 6, which estimates how long money takes to double at 6%, not at the 8% rate in the question.

prompt: The CPI stood at 250 one year ago and stands at 260 today. The inflation rate over that year is

options.text: 2.5 percent
3.8 percent
4.0 percent
10.0 percent

explanation: Inflation is the percentage change in the price index, using the starting index as the base. (260 minus 250) divided by 250 equals 10 divided by 250, or 4.0%.

distractorExplanations.a: Divides the 10-point rise by 400 instead of by the starting CPI of 250, so the percentage change is understated at 2.5%.
distractorExplanations.b: Divides the 10-point rise by the ending index of 260. The percentage change uses the beginning index of 250 as the base.
distractorExplanations.d: Reports the 10-point change in the index as though it were already a 10% rate, without dividing by the starting level of 250.

prompt: A bank that is short of reserves borrows from the Federal Reserve discount window. The rate on that loan is called the

options.text: Federal funds rate charged by other banks on overnight loans
Stop-out yield from the Treasury's latest bill auction
Discount rate set by the Federal Reserve
Prime rate the bank quotes to business customers

explanation: The discount rate is an administered rate on discount-window credit. It is what a depository institution pays when it borrows reserves directly from the Federal Reserve.

distractorExplanations.a: Names the federal funds rate, the overnight rate on reserve loans between banks, rather than the rate on a loan from the Fed itself.
distractorExplanations.b: Names a Treasury bill yield set in an auction of government debt, not the rate the Fed charges banks at the discount window.
distractorExplanations.d: Names the prime rate, a customer lending benchmark, rather than the rate on reserves borrowed from the Federal Reserve.

prompt: Under the expenditure approach, gross domestic product equals consumption, investment, government purchases, and which other term?

options.text: Corporate retained earnings for the year
The money supply multiplied by velocity
Net exports, meaning exports minus imports
Household saving minus capital consumption

explanation: The expenditure identity is GDP equals consumption plus investment plus government purchases plus net exports. Net exports are exports minus imports.

distractorExplanations.a: Retained earnings are an internal corporate funding source, not the foreign-trade term that completes the expenditure identity.
distractorExplanations.b: Money times velocity is the equation of exchange, a link to nominal spending, not the fourth term added to consumption, investment, and government.
distractorExplanations.d: Saving and depreciation relate to income and the capital stock. They are not the net-export term in the expenditure approach.

prompt: All else equal, a rise in imports that widens the trade deficit changes measured GDP in which way?

options.text: It raises net exports and therefore raises GDP
It leaves GDP unchanged because imports are omitted
It lowers net exports and therefore lowers GDP
It raises government purchases by the same dollar amount

explanation: Net exports equal exports minus imports, and GDP includes that term. If imports rise and nothing else changes, net exports fall, so measured GDP falls.

distractorExplanations.a: Reverses the sign of the trade term. Extra imports reduce net exports, so they do not raise the trade balance or GDP.
distractorExplanations.b: Imports are not omitted. They enter the accounts as a subtraction through net exports, so a rise in imports changes GDP.
distractorExplanations.d: A wider trade deficit does not automatically increase government purchases. Government spending is a separate term from net exports.

prompt: The Federal Reserve lifts its federal funds target from 4.50% to 5.25%. That step is best classified as

options.text: Expansionary fiscal policy enacted by Congress
Contractionary fiscal policy enacted by Congress
Contractionary monetary policy by the central bank
An automatic stabilizer that reduces tax rates

explanation: Raising the federal funds target from 4.50% to 5.25% makes reserve borrowing more expensive and restrains credit. That is contractionary monetary policy by the Fed.

distractorExplanations.a: A higher policy rate is a Fed action, not a congressional change in taxes or spending, and it restrains demand rather than adding to it.
distractorExplanations.b: Fiscal contraction would be a tax increase or a spending cut by Congress. Moving the funds target is monetary policy, not fiscal policy.
distractorExplanations.d: Automatic stabilizers, such as lower tax collections in a downturn, are fiscal and move without a new rate decision. This is a deliberate Fed increase.

prompt: Net income is $80,000 and sales are $800,000. The net profit margin is

options.text: 1 percent
8 percent
10 percent
80 percent

explanation: Net profit margin divides net income by sales. $80,000 divided by $800,000 equals 0.10, so 10 cents of each sales dollar remains as profit after expenses.

distractorExplanations.a: Divides $80,000 by $8,000,000, slipping an extra zero into sales, which produces 1% instead of the 10% margin.
distractorExplanations.b: Matches an 8% margin, which would require net income of $64,000 on these sales, not the $80,000 stated in the question.
distractorExplanations.d: Divides 80 by 100 rather than $80,000 by $800,000, shifting the decimal point and reporting 80% instead of 10%.

prompt: A client places $20,000 in an account that pays 6% simple interest per year. After three years the balance is
explanation: Simple interest each year is $20,000 times 6%, or $1,200, and that interest does not itself earn interest. Over three years the interest is $3,600, so the balance is $23,600.

distractorExplanations.a: Stops at the original $20,000 principal and credits none of the 6% simple interest earned across the three years.
distractorExplanations.b: Adds only one year of 6% interest, or $1,200, and leaves out the interest for the second and third years.
distractorExplanations.c: Adds two years of interest, or $2,400, and stops one year short of the three-year period stated in the question.

prompt: Cyclical unemployment is best described as joblessness that

options.text: Comes from short gaps while people move between jobs
Comes from a lasting mismatch between skills and openings
Counts retirees who have left the labor force entirely
Rises in a contraction and falls during an expansion

explanation: Cyclical unemployment is the part of joblessness tied to the business cycle. It increases when the economy contracts and demand for labor falls, then shrinks in an expansion.

distractorExplanations.a: Describes frictional unemployment from ordinary job search and turnover, which remains even when the economy is at full employment.
distractorExplanations.b: Describes structural unemployment from a skills or location mismatch, not the rise and fall in joblessness that follows the cycle.
distractorExplanations.c: Retirees are outside the labor force, so they are not counted as unemployed, whether the unemployment is cyclical or not.

prompt: If the marginal propensity to consume is 0.75, the simple spending multiplier is
explanation: The simple spending multiplier equals 1 divided by 1 minus the marginal propensity to consume. With an MPC of 0.75, saving out of an extra dollar is 0.25, and 1 divided by 0.25 equals 4.

distractorExplanations.a: Stops at the 0.75 marginal propensity to consume and never takes the reciprocal of the 0.25 share that is not spent.
distractorExplanations.b: Inverts the MPC itself, computing 1 divided by 0.75, instead of inverting 1 minus the MPC.
distractorExplanations.c: Adds 1 to the 0.75 MPC. The multiplier formula is 1 divided by 1 minus the MPC, not 1 plus the MPC.

prompt: In short-term business lending, the prime rate is best described as the

options.text: Overnight rate on reserve loans between commercial banks
Rate the Fed charges banks that borrow at the discount window
Yield fixed by statute on newly auctioned 10-year notes
Benchmark rate banks quote to their most creditworthy borrowers

explanation: The prime rate is a reference rate banks publish for loans to their strongest business customers. It tends to follow the federal funds rate, but banks set the quote rather than the Fed administering it directly.

distractorExplanations.a: Describes the federal funds rate on overnight loans of reserves between banks, not the customer lending benchmark called prime.
distractorExplanations.b: Describes the discount rate on borrowing from the Federal Reserve, which is not the prime rate quoted to bank customers.
distractorExplanations.c: The 10-year Treasury yield is set in the auction market, not by statute, and it is not the prime rate banks quote to borrowers.

prompt: When analysts say the Treasury yield curve is flat, they mean that

options.text: Short-term Treasury yields sit well above long-term yields
Long-term Treasury yields sit well above short-term yields
Treasury yields at each maturity equal the discount rate
Short-term and long-term Treasury yields are roughly equal

explanation: A flat curve has almost no slope, so moving from a short Treasury to a long one adds little extra yield. An upward slope would pay more for the longer maturity, and an inversion would pay more for the shorter one.

distractorExplanations.a: Short yields well above long yields describe an inverted curve, not a flat curve with yields about equal across maturities.
distractorExplanations.b: Long yields well above short yields describe a normal upward-sloping curve, not a flat curve.
distractorExplanations.c: The Fed does not peg every Treasury maturity to the discount rate. A flat curve is a market result, not an administered setting of each yield.

prompt: Demand-pull inflation is most likely in which of the following situations?

options.text: A supply disruption raises production costs across many industries
Household spending falls while the money supply stays unchanged
Imports rise sharply while domestic spending is contracting
Total spending grows faster than the economy can produce

explanation: Demand-pull inflation occurs when aggregate spending outruns what the economy can produce at current prices, so buyers bid the general price level higher.

distractorExplanations.a: Describes cost-push inflation from a supply shock, in which higher production costs push prices up rather than excess spending.
distractorExplanations.b: Falling household spending, with no increase in the money supply, relieves price pressure instead of pulling the price level up.
distractorExplanations.c: More imports and weaker domestic spending reduce pressure on domestic capacity, which is the opposite of demand-pull inflation.

prompt: Laura expects interest rates to rise sharply and holds a 20-year zero-coupon Treasury. She wants to cut interest-rate risk the most while keeping Treasury credit quality. Which swap fits?

options.text: A 20-year Treasury bond paying a 5% semiannual coupon
A 30-year Treasury Inflation-Protected Security (TIPS)
A 10-year zero-coupon Treasury STRIPS position
A 3-year Treasury note paying a 4% coupon

explanation: Interest-rate risk rises with duration. A zero's duration equals its maturity, so the 20-year zero carries about 20 years of duration. A 3-year coupon note has a duration under 3 years, the smallest here, so its price falls least when rates climb.

distractorExplanations.a: The coupon trims duration only modestly; a 20-year coupon bond still has a duration in the low teens and stays highly rate-sensitive.
distractorExplanations.b: TIPS adjust principal for inflation, but a 30-year maturity keeps duration very long, so rising real rates still hit price hard.
distractorExplanations.c: Halving the zero's maturity helps, but a 10-year zero still has a 10-year duration, far above a 3-year note.
