A claim on assets ahead of unsecured bondholders
Voting rights and residual claim on assets after creditors

explanation: Common stockholders vote for the board and stand last in line for the company's assets. Creditors, including unsecured bondholders, are paid before them, and whatever remains after those claims is the common stockholders' residual claim.

distractorExplanations.a: Preferred stockholders receive dividends before common stockholders, not after.
distractorExplanations.b: Common dividends are discretionary and variable; a fixed stated dividend is a preferred feature.
distractorExplanations.c: Common stockholders rank last, behind every class of creditor including unsecured bondholders.

prompt: A corporate bondholder is primarily exposed to

options.text: Credit risk and interest-rate risk
Guaranteed principal growth regardless of issuer health
Voting control of the issuer's board
FDIC insurance on the bond's face value

explanation: A corporate bondholder can lose interest or principal if the issuer defaults, and a rise in market yields pushes the price of a fixed coupon down before maturity. Credit risk and interest-rate risk are the two exposures that drive the bond's return.

distractorExplanations.b: The option treats principal as guaranteed growth. A corporate bond promises repayment only if the issuer pays, and a default can leave the holder with less than face value.
distractorExplanations.c: Electing directors is a common-stock right. A bondholder is a creditor of the issuer and does not receive a vote on the board.
distractorExplanations.d: FDIC insurance covers deposits at banks, not corporate bonds, so a bond's face value is not a deposit-insurance claim.

prompt: A limit order to buy stock specifies which of the following?

options.text: Execution at any price regardless of market
The maximum price the buyer is willing to pay
A minimum sale price for the seller
Cancellation only after one trading day by law

explanation: A buy limit states the highest price the buyer will pay. The order may fill at that price or at a lower one, and it stays unfilled if the market never trades at the limit or below it.

distractorExplanations.a: Limit orders cap price; they do not accept any price.
distractorExplanations.c: A minimum sale price is a sell limit, the floor a seller will accept. This order is a buy, so the limit is the most the buyer will pay, not the least a seller will take.
distractorExplanations.d: Time-in-force rules vary; there is no universal one-day limit.

prompt: A put option gives the holder the right to

options.text: Buy the underlying asset at the strike price before or at expiration
Receive the premium if the underlying stays above the strike
Sell the underlying at the strike price before or at expiration
Sell the underlying at the market price on expiration day

explanation: A put gives the holder the right, not the obligation, to sell the shares at the strike. That locked sale price is what cuts the loss when the market falls, which is why the put is used to hedge stock the client already owns.

distractorExplanations.a: The right to buy at the strike describes a call option, not a put.
distractorExplanations.b: Keeping the premium when the price stays above the strike is the put writer's outcome, not the holder's.
distractorExplanations.d: A put locks in the strike price; selling at the market price needs no option.

prompt: Closed-end funds differ from open-end mutual funds because closed-end funds

options.text: Redeem shares daily at NAV with the fund company
Continuously issue new shares as investors buy in
Trade on exchanges at prices fixed to their NAV
Trade on exchanges at prices that can differ from NAV

explanation: Closed-end shares are traded between investors on an exchange, and supply and demand set the price. The fund does not stand ready to redeem at net asset value, so the market price can sit at a premium or a discount to NAV.

distractorExplanations.a: Open-end funds redeem at NAV; closed-end funds generally do not.
distractorExplanations.b: Continuous issuance of new shares is an open-end fund feature; closed-end funds have a fixed share count.
distractorExplanations.c: Closed-end market prices float and often sit at a premium or discount to NAV.

prompt: A convertible bond allows the holder to do which of the following?

options.text: Exchange the bond for a predetermined number of shares
Exchange the bond for cash at par before maturity
Receive a coupon that resets with a benchmark rate
Buy additional shares at a set price via attached warrants

explanation: A convertible bond lets the holder turn the bond in for a set number of the issuer's shares. Until that exchange, the bond keeps paying its coupon, so the position is debt with a built-in right to become equity.

distractorExplanations.b: Redeeming for cash at par before maturity is a put feature of putable bonds, not conversion.
distractorExplanations.c: A coupon that resets with a benchmark describes a floating-rate note, not a convertible.
distractorExplanations.d: Warrants are separate purchase rights; a convertible exchanges the bond itself for shares.

prompt: Inverse exchange-traded funds (ETFs) are designed to:

options.text: Match long-term buy-and-hold index returns exactly
Deliver the opposite of a benchmark's daily return
Eliminate volatility over multi-year periods
Pay tax-exempt interest like municipals

explanation: An inverse ETF is built to deliver the opposite of its benchmark for that single day, and then the exposure resets. Compounding those daily resets means a holding of many months is not the simple opposite of the index over the whole period.

distractorExplanations.a: Matching the index's long-run gain is what a long index fund attempts. An inverse ETF targets the opposite of the daily return, and the daily reset keeps the long-run path from equaling the index.
distractorExplanations.c: The daily reset does not remove volatility. Rebalancing to the inverse each day can make a multi-year holding swing more than the index, rather than smoothing the path.
distractorExplanations.d: An inverse ETF does not pay tax-exempt municipal interest; its payoff is the opposite of a benchmark's daily return.

prompt: Junk bonds are characterized by which of the following features?

options.text: Investment-grade ratings and higher yield spreads
Non-investment-grade ratings and lower yield spreads
Non-investment-grade ratings and higher yield spreads
Ratings of BBB or above with low default rates

explanation: Lower-rated issuers pay higher yields to compensate for elevated credit risk. The extra yield pays for default risk; it is not a free increase in return after losses.

distractorExplanations.a: Junk bonds are below investment grade; investment-grade issuers pay narrower spreads.
distractorExplanations.b: Investors demand wider, not narrower, yield spreads to hold non-investment-grade credit.
distractorExplanations.d: BBB-/Baa3 and above is investment grade; junk bonds are rated BB+/Ba1 or lower.

prompt: A master limited partnership (MLP) primarily operates in

options.text: Commercial real estate such as office towers
Technology and biotech venture investments
Municipal water and transit infrastructure
Energy and natural-resource infrastructure

explanation: MLPs often own pipelines and pass income to unit holders with unique tax reporting. MLPs use pass-through taxation, so unit holders receive Schedule K-1s.

distractorExplanations.a: Commercial real estate ownership is the domain of REITs, not master limited partnerships.
distractorExplanations.b: MLPs must earn qualifying income, largely from natural resources, not venture technology investments.
distractorExplanations.c: Municipal water and transit projects are financed by muni bonds, not structured as MLPs.

prompt: Structured notes may expose investors to

options.text: Issuer credit risk plus embedded derivative payoff formulas
FDIC insurance on principal up to $250,000 per depositor
Principal protection backed by the U.S. Treasury
SIPC coverage against the issuer's default

explanation: A structured note's payoff follows a formula tied to an index or other reference, which is a derivative embedded in the note, and the note itself is the issuer's unsecured debt. The investor can lose money from the formula or from the issuer's default.

distractorExplanations.b: Structured notes are unsecured issuer debt; FDIC insurance covers bank deposits, not these notes.
distractorExplanations.c: Any principal protection depends on the issuer's credit, not on U.S. Treasury backing.
distractorExplanations.d: SIPC covers missing customer assets at a failed broker-dealer, not losses from issuer default.

prompt: A fixed annuity contract typically provides

options.text: Tax-free growth and withdrawals after age 59½
Tax-deferred growth and insurer-guaranteed minimum interest
Tax-deferred growth and returns tied to subaccount performance
SIPC protection on cash value like a brokerage account

explanation: Earnings inside a fixed annuity are tax-deferred, and the insurer credits interest at no less than the contract's guaranteed minimum rate. That credit does not come from a market subaccount, and it depends on the insurer's ability to pay.

distractorExplanations.a: Tax-free qualified withdrawals describe a Roth IRA; annuity gains are taxed as ordinary income.
distractorExplanations.c: Returns tied to subaccounts describe a variable annuity, not a fixed annuity.
distractorExplanations.d: SIPC covers broker-dealer failures; fixed annuity guarantees depend on the insurer's claims-paying ability.

prompt: Exchange-traded notes (ETNs) differ from ETFs because ETN holders face

options.text: Daily redemption at NAV from an independent trust of assets
Insurance guarantees from state guaranty funds on the trading price
Unsecured credit exposure to the issuing bank
No tracking of any index or strategy

explanation: ETNs are senior unsecured debt obligations whose value depends on issuer credit and index performance.

distractorExplanations.a: ETNs are notes, not baskets of assets redeemable like open-end funds.
distractorExplanations.b: Guaranty funds cover certain insurance products, not ETN trading losses.
distractorExplanations.d: An ETN is written to track a stated index or strategy, so the claim that it tracks nothing reverses the product's design.

prompt: When interest rates rise, an existing bond with a fixed coupon generally

options.text: Rises in price because coupons become more valuable automatically
Keeps the same market price until maturity regardless of rates
Converts to equity at the new market rate
Falls in price because new issues offer higher yields

explanation: A fixed coupon becomes less attractive when market yields rise, so the existing bond's price falls until its yield matches the higher yields on new issues.

distractorExplanations.a: Higher rates make existing lower coupons less attractive, pressuring price.
distractorExplanations.b: The price is not locked until maturity. When market yields rise, secondary-market buyers pay less for the old lower coupon, so the bond's price falls before it matures.
distractorExplanations.c: A rise in rates does not convert a conventional bond into stock. Conversion belongs to a convertible bond, and the holder chooses it; the new market yield does not trigger it.

prompt: A covered call strategy on stock the client owns involves

options.text: Selling call options to generate premium income while capping upside
Buying put options to protect against a decline in the stock
Selling put options to collect premium and possibly buy more of the shares
Writing calls without owning the stock to collect premium income

explanation: Covered calls exchange some upside for premium; downside remains except to the extent premium offsets losses.

distractorExplanations.b: Buying puts against owned stock is a protective put, a hedge, not a covered call.
distractorExplanations.c: Selling puts to possibly acquire shares is a cash-secured put strategy, not a covered call.
distractorExplanations.d: Writing calls without the stock is a naked (uncovered) call with unlimited risk.

prompt: Contingent deferred sales charges (CDSC) in mutual funds

options.text: Increase the longer shares are held before redemption
Decline over time and may apply on redemptions within a stated period
Are deducted from each purchase as a front-end load
Are annual 12b-1 fees charged for distribution and marketing costs

explanation: B-share and similar structures often assess declining back-end loads on early redemptions. The charge falls as the holding period lengthens, unlike an A-share front-end load.

distractorExplanations.a: Reverses the schedule; CDSC percentages decline the longer shares are held.
distractorExplanations.c: Charges deducted at purchase are front-end loads (Class A), not contingent deferred charges.
distractorExplanations.d: 12b-1 fees are ongoing annual distribution fees, separate from a back-end CDSC on redemption.

prompt: A client in the 32% federal bracket, ignoring state tax, compares a municipal bond yielding 4.2% with a taxable corporate bond yielding 5.8% of similar maturity and credit. The municipal bond's taxable-equivalent yield is closest to:

options.text: 6.18%, the 4.2% yield divided by (1 − 0.32)
4.2%, because a municipal yield is already stated on a taxable basis
2.86%, the 4.2% yield multiplied by (1 − 0.32)
5.54%, the 4.2% yield multiplied by 1.32

explanation: Taxable-equivalent yield equals the tax-exempt yield divided by one minus the marginal tax rate. Here 4.2% ÷ (1 − 0.32) = 4.2% ÷ 0.68 ≈ 6.18%. That grossed-up figure is what a taxable bond must yield to match the muni for this investor.

distractorExplanations.b: Leaving the yield at 4.2% skips the tax gross-up. Municipal interest is exempt, so the comparable taxable yield is 4.2% divided by 0.68, not the coupon itself.
distractorExplanations.c: Multiplying 4.2% by (1 − 0.32) shrinks it to about 2.86%. The taxable-equivalent formula divides by (1 − tax rate); it does not multiply by that factor.
distractorExplanations.d: Multiplying 4.2% by 1.32 produces about 5.54% and adds the tax rate on top of the yield. The correct gross-up divides by 0.68, which is about 6.18%.

prompt: A bond with a $1,000 par value pays a 6% annual coupon and trades at $960. Its current yield is closest to:

options.text: 6.00%, the annual coupon divided by the $1,000 par value
6.25%, the $60 annual coupon divided by the $960 price
4.00%, the $40 discount from par divided by the $1,000 face value
5.76%, the 6% coupon multiplied by the $960 price over par

explanation: Current yield is the annual coupon payment divided by the bond's current market price, not by par. A 6% coupon on $1,000 pays $60 a year, and $60 ÷ $960 = 6.25%. Because the bond is priced at a discount, current yield sits above the coupon rate.

distractorExplanations.a: The 6.00% figure divides the $60 coupon by par. Current yield divides that same $60 by the $960 market price, which is 6.25%.
distractorExplanations.c: The $40 discount divided by par is 4%, a price gap rather than income. Current yield uses the $60 coupon in the numerator and the $960 price in the denominator.
distractorExplanations.d: Multiplying the 6% coupon by 960/1,000 produces 5.76% and moves the yield the wrong way. Dividing the $60 coupon by the lower $960 price raises the yield to 6.25%.

prompt: A 10-year corporate bond has a 4% annual coupon. New 10-year bonds of similar credit yield 6%. Relative to its $1,000 par, this bond should trade at:

options.text: A premium, because the 4% coupon is a contractual cash payment
Par, because the 10-year maturity matches the new 10-year issues
A discount, because the 4% coupon is below the 6% market yield
A premium equal to the 2-point gap between the 6% yield and the 4% coupon

explanation: A fixed-coupon bond is priced by discounting its cash flows at the yield investors currently require. When the coupon, 4%, is below that market yield, 6%, buyers pay less than the $1,000 par so the discount lifts their return to 6%. Price and yield move in opposite directions.

distractorExplanations.a: A contractual coupon does not create a premium. A premium requires the coupon to exceed the market yield, and this 4% coupon is below the 6% yield.
distractorExplanations.b: Matching the 10-year maturity only sets the comparison. The bond trades at par when its coupon equals the 6% market yield, which this 4% coupon does not.
distractorExplanations.d: The 2-point gap is why buyers demand a lower price, not a higher one. A coupon below the market yield produces a discount to the $1,000 par.

prompt: A call option has a $50 strike. The stock trades at $58, and the call premium is $11. The call's intrinsic value is:

options.text: $11, the full premium quoted in the market
$3, the premium minus the amount by which $58 exceeds $50
$0, because intrinsic value is counted on expiration day
$8, the amount by which the $58 price exceeds the $50 strike

explanation: Intrinsic value of a call is the greater of zero and the stock price minus the strike. With the stock at $58 and a $50 strike, intrinsic value is $8. The $11 premium is that $8 plus $3 of time value, and time value is not part of intrinsic value.

distractorExplanations.a: The $11 premium packages intrinsic value and time value together. Only $8 is intrinsic; the other $3 is time value that can decay before expiration.
distractorExplanations.b: Subtracting the $8 in-the-money amount from the $11 premium isolates the $3 of time value. Intrinsic value is the $8 stock-over-strike amount, not the leftover $3.
distractorExplanations.c: Intrinsic value is measured whenever the option is alive, not only at expiration. A call with the stock $8 above the strike already has $8 of intrinsic value.

prompt: An open-end mutual fund holds portfolio assets of $42 million, has liabilities of $1 million, and has 4 million shares outstanding. Its NAV per share is:

options.text: $10.75, assets plus liabilities divided by the 4 million shares
$42.00, the $42 million of assets divided by the $1 million of liabilities
$10.25, net assets of $41 million divided by 4 million shares
$10.50, the $42 million of assets divided by 4 million shares

explanation: Net asset value per share equals portfolio assets minus liabilities, divided by shares outstanding. Here ($42 million − $1 million) ÷ 4 million shares = $10.25. Open-end funds transact with shareholders at this NAV, so the liability has to come out before the division.

distractorExplanations.a: Adding the $1 million liability to the $42 million of assets produces $43 million and a $10.75 figure. Liabilities are subtracted from assets, not added.
distractorExplanations.b: Dividing $42 million of assets by $1 million of liabilities gives a ratio of 42, not a per-share price. NAV divides net assets by the 4 million shares.
distractorExplanations.d: Dividing the $42 million of gross assets by 4 million shares is $10.50 and skips the liability. Net assets are $41 million, so NAV is $10.25.

prompt: A preferred stock with a $25 par value pays a $1.75 annual dividend and trades at $28. Its current dividend yield is closest to:

options.text: 7.00%, the $1.75 dividend divided by the $25 par value
6.25%, the $1.75 dividend divided by the $28 market price
12.00%, the $3 premium over par divided by the $25 par value
1.75%, the dollar dividend stated as a percent without using price

explanation: Current yield on preferred stock is the annual dividend divided by the current market price, the same idea as a bond's current yield. Here $1.75 ÷ $28 = 6.25%. Par is used to state the dividend rate at issue, not the yield an investor earns at today's $28 price.

distractorExplanations.a: Dividing $1.75 by the $25 par gives the 7% stated rate. An investor who pays $28 earns $1.75 on $28, which is 6.25%, not 7%.
distractorExplanations.c: The $3 premium over par divided by $25 is 12%, and that premium is a price gap, not a dividend. Yield uses the $1.75 cash dividend over the $28 price.
distractorExplanations.d: Writing the $1.75 dividend as 1.75% treats dollars as a percent. The yield divides that cash dividend by the $28 market price, which is 6.25%.

prompt: A 15-year zero-coupon Treasury is priced at $482 per $1,000 of face value and pays nothing until maturity. Its Macaulay duration, in years, is closest to:

options.text: 7.5 years, half of the 15-year maturity because the bond pays no coupon
4.82 years, the $482 price divided by 100
15 years, equal to maturity because the only cash flow is the face amount
10 years, a duration ceiling applied to Treasury zeros of every maturity

explanation: Macaulay duration is the present-value-weighted average time until cash flows are received. A zero pays its only cash flow at maturity, so every dollar of value arrives at year 15 and duration equals 15 years. The $482 discount changes the yield, not the timing of that single payment.

distractorExplanations.a: Halving the maturity would be a rough shortcut for a coupon bond. With no coupons, nothing pulls this zero's duration below its 15-year maturity.
distractorExplanations.b: Dividing the $482 price by 100 restates the price as 4.82. Duration here is the year of the single cash flow, which is year 15.
distractorExplanations.d: Treasury zeros have no 10-year duration ceiling. This bond's only cash flow is the face amount at year 15, so Macaulay duration is 15 years.

prompt: A convertible bond with a $1,000 par amount converts into 25 shares of common stock. The stock trades at $36. The bond's conversion value is:

options.text: $900, equal to 25 shares times the $36 stock price
$1,000, the par amount paid if the bond is held to maturity
$100, the difference between the $1,000 par and 25 times $36
$25, the conversion ratio stated as a dollar amount

explanation: Conversion value equals the conversion ratio times the current stock price. Twenty-five shares at $36 are worth $900, so converting today produces $900 of stock. The bond's market price is ordinarily at least this conversion value, or investors would buy the bond and sell the stock.

distractorExplanations.b: The $1,000 par is the cash claim if the bond is held as debt to maturity. Conversion value is the stock package, 25 × $36, which is $900.
distractorExplanations.c: Subtracting $900 from the $1,000 par measures how far conversion value sits below face. The conversion value itself is the $900 of stock.
distractorExplanations.d: The conversion ratio is a count of 25 shares, not a dollar price. Dollar conversion value multiplies those 25 shares by the $36 stock price.

prompt: An investor buys 100 shares at $40 and sells one $45 call for a $2 premium. At expiration the stock is $52 and the call is exercised. Profit on the covered position is:

options.text: $1,200, the $12 rise from $40 to $52 on all 100 shares
$200, limited to the $2 premium collected on the one call
$700, a $500 gain from $40 up to the $45 strike plus the $200 premium
$500, the gain from $40 to the $45 strike, with the premium left out

explanation: A covered call keeps the premium and, if assigned, sells the stock at the strike. The stock gain is capped at $45 − $40 = $5, or $500 on 100 shares, and the $2 premium adds $200, for a $700 profit. The move from $45 to $52 belongs to the call holder, not the covered writer.

distractorExplanations.a: The $12 rise from $40 to $52 would be the gain on shares with no call written. The $45 call gives the extra $7 per share, or $700 of that move, to the call holder.
distractorExplanations.b: The $200 premium is only part of the result. Assignment also sells the shares at $45, locking in a $5 per share gain on the $40 cost.
distractorExplanations.d: The $500 stock gain up to the strike drops the $200 premium the writer keeps. Both the capped stock gain and the premium are part of the $700 profit.

prompt: A put option has a $40 strike and trades at a $9 premium while the stock is at $33. The put's intrinsic value is:

options.text: $9, the full premium quoted for the put
$2, the $9 premium minus the gap between the $40 strike and the $33 price
$0, because a put has intrinsic value when the stock is above the strike
$7, the amount by which the $40 strike exceeds the $33 stock price

explanation: Intrinsic value of a put is the greater of zero and the strike minus the stock price. A $40 strike with the stock at $33 is $7 in the money. The $9 premium is that $7 plus $2 of time value. A put gains intrinsic value when the stock falls below the strike, which is the case here.

distractorExplanations.a: The $9 premium includes both intrinsic value and time value. Only $7 is intrinsic; the other $2 is time value that can disappear as expiration approaches.
distractorExplanations.b: Subtracting the $7 in-the-money amount from the $9 premium isolates the $2 of time value. Intrinsic value is the $7 strike-over-stock amount, not the leftover $2.
distractorExplanations.c: A put has intrinsic value when the stock is below the strike, not above it. At $33 versus a $40 strike, intrinsic value is $7, not zero.

prompt: A closed-end fund reports an NAV of $20 a share, and the shares trade on the exchange at $17. The fund is trading at a:

options.text: 15% premium, because an investor can buy the shares for $17
15% discount, because $17 is $3 below the $20 NAV
3% discount, the $3 price gap divided by $100
Price equal to NAV, because exchange trading resets the price to $20

explanation: A closed-end fund's market price is set by exchange supply and demand and can sit away from NAV. The discount is (NAV − price) ÷ NAV = ($20 − $17) ÷ $20 = 15%. Buyers pay $17 for $20 of net assets, and the fund does not redeem those shares at the $20 NAV.

distractorExplanations.a: A premium would require the $17 market price to exceed the $20 NAV. The price is $3 below NAV, so the gap is a 15% discount.
distractorExplanations.c: The $3 gap is 15% of the $20 NAV, not 3% of an assumed $100. The discount percentage uses NAV as the denominator.
distractorExplanations.d: Exchange trading is why the price can leave NAV. These shares are not redeemed at $20, so a $17 print is a 15% discount.

prompt: A 5-year TIPS note has a 1.5% real coupon and $1,000 of principal. Over the year, the CPI index used to adjust the note rises 3%. The adjusted principal becomes:

options.text: $1,000, because Treasury principal stays fixed until maturity
$1,015, the original principal increased by the 1.5% real coupon
$1,030, the $1,000 principal increased by the 3% CPI change
$1,045, the principal increased by the 1.5% coupon plus the 3% CPI change

explanation: TIPS adjust principal for inflation, and the stated coupon is a real rate applied to that adjusted principal. A 3% rise in the CPI index lifts $1,000 of principal to $1,030. The 1.5% coupon is then paid on the adjusted principal; it is not added into the principal adjustment itself.

distractorExplanations.a: Nominal Treasuries keep principal fixed at $1,000. TIPS reset principal with the CPI index, so a 3% index rise moves this note's principal to $1,030.
distractorExplanations.b: The 1.5% figure is the real coupon rate, not the inflation index. Principal moves with the 3% CPI change, to $1,030, and the coupon is paid on that new principal.
distractorExplanations.d: Adding the 1.5% coupon to the 3% CPI change double-counts. Principal is indexed by the 3% CPI change alone, which takes $1,000 to $1,030.

prompt: A stock just paid a $2.00 dividend. Dividends are expected to grow at 4% a year forever, and the required return is 10%. The constant-growth value is closest to:

options.text: $20.00, the $2.00 dividend divided by the 10% required return
$33.33, the $2.00 dividend just paid, divided by 10% minus 4%
$34.67, next year's $2.08 dividend divided by 10% minus 4%
$50.00, the $2.00 dividend divided by the 4% growth rate

explanation: The constant-growth model prices a stock as next year's dividend divided by the required return minus the growth rate. The $2.00 dividend just paid must be grown one year, to $2.00 × 1.04 = $2.08. Then $2.08 ÷ (0.10 − 0.04) = $34.67. Growth is subtracted in the denominator, and it must stay below the required return.

distractorExplanations.a: Dividing the trailing $2.00 dividend by 10% skips both the growth to next year's $2.08 dividend and the subtraction of the 4% growth rate from the discount rate.
distractorExplanations.b: Dividing the $2.00 dividend just paid by 6% forgets to grow it. Next year's dividend is $2.08, and $2.08 ÷ (0.10 − 0.04) equals $34.67.
distractorExplanations.d: Dividing the $2.00 dividend by the 4% growth rate ignores the 10% required return. The denominator is required return minus growth, and the numerator is $2.08.

prompt: A company earned $4.00 per share over the last year, and the shares trade at $60. Its trailing price-to-earnings ratio is:

options.text: 240 times, the $60 price multiplied by the $4.00 of earnings
15 times, the $60 price divided by the $4.00 of trailing earnings
60 times, the share price used by itself as the earnings multiple
0.067 times, the $4.00 of earnings divided by the $60 price

explanation: The trailing price-to-earnings ratio divides the current share price by earnings per share over the last year. Here $60 ÷ $4.00 = 15, so the shares trade at 15 times recent earnings. The reciprocal, $4.00 ÷ $60, is the earnings yield, not the P/E multiple.

distractorExplanations.a: Multiplying the $60 price by $4.00 of earnings gives 240, which is not a ratio of price to earnings. Trailing P/E divides price by earnings: $60 ÷ $4.00 = 15.
distractorExplanations.c: The $60 price is the numerator of the ratio, not the ratio itself. Dividing that price by the $4.00 of earnings produces a multiple of 15.
distractorExplanations.d: Dividing $4.00 of earnings by the $60 price gives the 0.067 earnings yield. The P/E multiple is the reciprocal, $60 ÷ $4.00 = 15.

prompt: A client buys a share at $50 and buys a $50 put on it for a $3 premium. At expiration the stock is $42 and the client exercises the put. The net loss per share is:

options.text: $8, the decline from the $50 purchase price to the $42 market price
$11, the $8 price decline added to the $3 premium
$0, because the $50 put restores the full $50 purchase price with nothing left over
$3, the premium, because exercise sells the share at the $50 cost

explanation: A protective put sets a sale floor at the strike. With the strike equal to the $50 cost, exercising the put sells the share at $50 and cancels the $8 market decline from $50 to $42. The client still paid a $3 premium for that floor, so the net loss is $3 per share.

distractorExplanations.a: The $8 decline from $50 to $42 is the move the put was bought to offset. Exercise sells the share at the $50 strike, and the remaining loss is the $3 premium.
distractorExplanations.b: Adding the $3 premium on top of the $8 decline counts the market loss that exercise removes. Selling at the $50 strike cancels that $8, leaving the $3 premium.
distractorExplanations.c: The put does sell the share at the $50 purchase price, but the protection cost $3. That premium is a cash loss, so the position does not finish flat.

prompt: A cumulative preferred stock has a $5 annual dividend. The issuer skipped the preferred dividend for 2 years and now wants to pay a $1 common dividend. Before any common dividend, each preferred share must receive:

options.text: $15, the two missed $5 dividends plus this year's $5 dividend
$5, limited to the current year's stated preferred dividend
$10, the two skipped years, with this year's $5 dividend deferred
$1, the same dividend the board proposed for the common shares

explanation: Cumulative preferred dividends that are skipped stay in arrears and must be paid, together with the current preferred dividend, before common shareholders receive anything. Two missed years at $5 plus the current $5 equal $15 per preferred share. A noncumulative preferred would not carry the missed years forward.

distractorExplanations.b: Paying only this year's $5 ignores the cumulative feature. The two skipped $5 dividends are still owed and stand ahead of the proposed $1 common dividend.
distractorExplanations.c: The $10 of arrears has to be paid, and so does the current year's $5 dividend. Both are senior to common, so the preferred share must receive $15.
distractorExplanations.d: Matching the $1 common dividend reverses the payment order. Common cannot be paid until the $10 of arrears and the current $5 preferred dividend are cleared.

prompt: A corporation issues $5 million of commercial paper maturing in 90 days to finance inventory. This paper is best classified as:

options.text: Equity, because the firm is raising $5 million of business capital
A capital-market bond, because a $5 million borrowing is long-term debt
A money market instrument, because the maturity is 90 days
A Treasury bill, because a 90-day discount obligation is government paper

explanation: Money market instruments are high-quality debt maturing in one year or less. Commercial paper is the issuer's own unsecured short-term note, and 90 days is inside that one-year line, so this $5 million issue is a money market instrument. The dollar size describes how much was borrowed, not which market the paper belongs to.

distractorExplanations.a: The corporation is borrowing $5 million, not selling ownership. Commercial paper is a debt obligation that must be repaid in 90 days.
distractorExplanations.b: Capital-market bonds mature beyond one year. A 90-day maturity keeps this paper in the money market no matter that the face amount is $5 million.
distractorExplanations.d: Treasury bills are obligations of the U.S. Treasury. This 90-day paper is the corporation's own note, so the credit risk is the issuer's, not the Treasury's.

prompt: A REIT has $10 million of taxable income for the year. To satisfy the annual distribution test for REIT tax treatment, it must distribute at least:

options.text: $5 million, half of taxable income, and may retain the rest untaxed
$9 million, which is 90% of the $10 million of taxable income
$10 million, the entire taxable income, because a 90% test does not exist
$0, because REIT income is exempt at the entity whether or not it is paid out

explanation: A REIT is allowed to deduct dividends paid, and it must distribute at least 90% of taxable income to qualify. On $10 million of taxable income the floor is 0.90 × $10 million = $9 million. Shareholders generally owe tax on the distributions they receive; the 90% figure is a payout test for the entity.

distractorExplanations.a: A $5 million, 50% payout fails the REIT distribution test. The required minimum is 90% of the $10 million of taxable income, which is $9 million.
distractorExplanations.c: Paying out all $10 million would more than meet the test, but the minimum is 90%, not 100%. The floor on this income is $9 million.
distractorExplanations.d: Undistributed REIT taxable income is taxed at the entity. The deduction depends on distributing at least $9 million, and shareholders still owe tax on what they receive.

prompt: A variable annuity has a $100,000 account value, all of it in an equity subaccount that falls 20%. There is no living-benefit rider, and no other credit or deduction applies. The account value is now:

options.text: $100,000, because the insurer guarantees the principal of this variable annuity
$120,000, because the account steps up by 20% when the equity subaccount falls
$80,000, because the owner bears the subaccount's 20% market decline
$97,000, because a variable annuity stops an equity loss at 3%

explanation: In a variable annuity the owner selects the subaccounts and bears their market results unless a rider provides a stated guarantee. A 20% decline on $100,000, with no living-benefit rider and no other credit or deduction, leaves $80,000. The insurer stands behind the contract's promises, not behind an unhedged equity subaccount.

distractorExplanations.a: A principal guarantee of that kind belongs to a fixed annuity or to a specific rider. This contract has no living-benefit rider, so the 20% equity decline reaches the $100,000 account.
distractorExplanations.b: An equity subaccount moves with the market. A 20% decline reduces $100,000 to $80,000; it does not step the account up to $120,000.
distractorExplanations.d: This contract has no 3% loss stop. Without a rider, the subaccount's own 20% decline takes the $100,000 account value to $80,000.

prompt: An indexed annuity credits the lesser of 60% of the index gain and a 7% annual cap. The linked index rises 20% during the year. The interest credited is:

options.text: 20%, the full index gain, because the contract is linked to that index
12%, equal to 60% of the 20% index gain, with the cap left unused
0%, because a rising index produces no credit on an indexed annuity
7%, because 60% of the 20% gain is 12% and the cap is lower

explanation: An indexed annuity credits interest from a formula rather than from ownership of the index. Participation of 60% times a 20% index gain would be 12%, but the contract credits the lesser of that result and the 7% cap. Because 12% is above 7%, the interest credited is 7%.

distractorExplanations.a: The contract does not pass through the 20% index gain. The 60% participation rate and the 7% cap both stand between the index and the interest actually credited.
distractorExplanations.b: Sixty percent of the 20% index gain is 12% before the cap. The contract credits the lesser of 12% and the 7% cap, so the cap binds and the credit is 7%.
distractorExplanations.c: A decline is when the credited rate can fall to the contract floor, often zero. This index rose 20%, so the credit is the capped upside of 7%, not zero.

prompt: A warrant lets the holder buy one share at an exercise price of $30. The common stock trades at $46, and the warrant trades at $19. The warrant's intrinsic value is:

options.text: $19, the price at which the warrant itself is trading
$16, the $46 stock price minus the $30 exercise price
$46, the full market price of the common stock
$30, the exercise price the warrant locks in

explanation: A warrant's intrinsic value is the greater of zero and the stock price minus the exercise price, the same arithmetic as a call. With the stock at $46 and a $30 exercise price, intrinsic value is $16. The $19 market price of the warrant is that $16 plus $3 of time value.

distractorExplanations.a: The $19 trading price is what buyers pay for the warrant. Intrinsic value is only the $16 by which the stock exceeds the exercise price; the extra $3 is time value.
distractorExplanations.c: The $46 stock price is the underlying asset, not the warrant's intrinsic value. Intrinsic value subtracts the $30 exercise price from that $46.
distractorExplanations.d: The $30 exercise price is what the holder must pay to receive the share. Intrinsic value is the $16 advantage of buying a $46 share for $30.

prompt: A firm is liquidated for $8 million. It owes $5 million to secured creditors and $2 million to unsecured bondholders, and it has no preferred stock. The amount left for common stockholders is:

options.text: $8 million, because the common stockholders own the liquidated firm
$3 million, the $8 million of proceeds minus the $5 million secured claim
$1 million, the proceeds left after both the $5 million and the $2 million of debt
$0, because common stockholders are paid ahead of the unsecured bondholders

explanation: In liquidation, creditors are paid before owners, and secured creditors are paid before unsecured creditors. The secured claim takes $5 million and the unsecured bonds take $2 million, leaving $8 million − $7 million = $1 million for common stock. Common has the residual claim, which is paid last.

distractorExplanations.a: Ownership does not put common first in line. The $8 million is applied to the $7 million of debt claims before any residual is left for the shares.
distractorExplanations.b: Stopping after the $5 million secured claim leaves the $2 million unsecured bond claim unpaid. Both debt classes come ahead of common, so the residual is not $3 million.
distractorExplanations.d: A zero residual would follow if debt exceeded the $8 million of proceeds. Debt here is $7 million, so common receives $1 million, and it is paid after the bondholders.

prompt: A bond with an 8% annual coupon on a $1,000 par is priced at $1,080. Comparable bonds yield 6% to maturity. This bond is:

options.text: A premium bond, because the 8% coupon is above the 6% market yield
A discount bond, because the price sits $80 away from the $1,000 par
A par bond, because it repays the $1,000 face amount at maturity
A zero-coupon bond, because the 6% yield is different from the 8% coupon

explanation: When a bond's coupon exceeds the yield investors require, buyers pay more than par. The 8% coupon is above the 6% market yield, and the $1,080 price is $80 above the $1,000 par, which is a premium. If the yield stays at 6%, that premium amortizes down toward par as maturity approaches.

distractorExplanations.b: A discount bond trades below par and carries a coupon below the market yield. This bond's $1,080 price is above the $1,000 par, and 8% is above the 6% yield.
distractorExplanations.c: Repaying $1,000 at maturity is true of a conventional option-free bond at any current price. Today's price is $1,080, so the bond is a premium bond, not a par bond.
distractorExplanations.d: A zero-coupon bond pays no coupon at all. This bond pays an 8% coupon; the gap versus the 6% yield is what makes the $1,080 price a premium.

prompt: A call has a $25 strike, the stock is $25, and the premium is $2.40 with 60 days left until expiration. The call's time value is:

options.text: $25.00, equal to the strike because the option is at the money
$0, because time value exists only after the stock moves above the strike
$2.40, the entire premium, because intrinsic value at a $25 stock price is zero
$27.40, the $25 strike added to the $2.40 premium

explanation: Time value equals the option premium minus intrinsic value. With the stock and the strike both at $25, the call is at the money and intrinsic value is zero, so the entire $2.40 premium is time value. Those 60 days are what the buyer is paying for: the chance the stock rises above $25.

distractorExplanations.a: The $25 strike is the exercise price, not the time value. With the stock also at $25, intrinsic value is zero and the $2.40 premium is all time value.
distractorExplanations.b: Time value is not reserved for options that are already in the money. This at-the-money call has zero intrinsic value, so its whole $2.40 premium is time value.
distractorExplanations.d: Adding the $25 strike to the $2.40 premium mixes the exercise price into the option's price. Time value is the premium minus intrinsic value, which here is $2.40.

prompt: A whole life policy has a $250,000 death benefit and a cash surrender value of $18,000 in year 8. If the owner surrenders the policy in year 8, the amount paid for that surrender is:

options.text: $250,000, because surrender advances the death benefit to the owner
$268,000, the $250,000 death benefit plus the $18,000 cash surrender value
$0, because the cash value is paid at death rather than on a living surrender
$18,000, the cash surrender value, and the $250,000 death benefit ends

explanation: Whole life combines a death benefit with a savings element that builds cash value. On a living surrender the owner receives the cash surrender value, here $18,000, and the $250,000 death benefit ends. The death benefit is paid to beneficiaries if the insured dies while the policy is in force; it is not stacked on top of a surrender.

distractorExplanations.a: The $250,000 is the amount payable at death, not the living surrender value. Surrender pays the $18,000 cash surrender value and cancels the death benefit.
distractorExplanations.b: Adding the death benefit to the cash surrender value would pay both at once. Surrender replaces the $250,000 death benefit with the $18,000 cash value.
distractorExplanations.c: The death benefit is what requires the insured's death. The $18,000 cash surrender value is the living amount the owner receives by surrendering in year 8.

prompt: An ADR represents 4 shares of a foreign company. Those local shares trade at $12 each, ignoring currency translation. The ADR's underlying share value is:

options.text: $12, the market price of one local share
$48, four local shares at $12 each
$3, the $12 local share price divided by the 4-share ratio
$16, the 4-share ratio added to the $12 local price

explanation: An ADR's ratio states how many local shares stand behind one receipt. With 4 local shares per ADR and each local share at $12, the receipt's underlying value is 4 × $12 = $48 before currency translation. One ADR is the economic package of four shares, not of a single share.

distractorExplanations.a: The $12 price is one local share. This ADR wraps 4 local shares, so the receipt's underlying value is 4 × $12 = $48, not the single-share price.
distractorExplanations.c: Dividing the $12 share price by 4 reverses the ratio. The ADR contains 4 shares, so the $12 price is multiplied by 4 to reach $48.
distractorExplanations.d: Adding the 4-share ratio to the $12 price mixes a share count with dollars. The dollar value is 4 times $12, which is $48.

prompt: A bond has a modified duration of 8. Yields then rise by 50 basis points. The approximate percentage change in the bond's price is:

options.text: Up 4%, because a higher yield increases the value of a fixed coupon
Down 8%, treating the 50-basis-point rise as a full 1% yield change
Down 4%, because a duration of 8 times a 0.50% yield rise is a 4% price decline
Down 0.50%, equal to the yield change, with duration left out of the estimate

explanation: Modified duration estimates the percentage price change as the negative of duration times the yield change stated in percent. A duration of 8 times a 0.50% yield increase is a 4% price decline. The sign is negative because a higher yield discounts the same coupons more heavily. The estimate is linear and less accurate for large moves.

distractorExplanations.a: The sign runs the wrong way. Raising the yield discounts the same coupons at a higher rate, so the price falls by about 4%; it does not rise.
distractorExplanations.b: Treating 50 basis points as a full 1% doubles the move. Duration of 8 times 0.50%, not times 1%, is a decline of about 4%.
distractorExplanations.d: The 0.50% figure is the yield change, not the price change. Duration scales it: 8 × 0.50% is a price decline of about 4%.

prompt: An investor buys a 180-day Treasury bill at $9,700 per $10,000 of face value. The bill pays no coupon. The dollar return if the bill is held to maturity is:

options.text: $300, the difference between the $10,000 face value and the $9,700 price
$0, because a bill that pays no coupon produces no investment return
$9,700, the purchase price, repaid on top of the $10,000 face value
$10,000, the full face amount, counted as profit rather than as a return of cash invested

explanation: Treasury bills are discount instruments. The buyer pays $9,700 and receives the $10,000 face value at maturity, so the dollar return is the $300 accretion of that discount. There is no coupon. The $10,000 receipt includes the investor's own $9,700, and only the $300 gap is profit.

distractorExplanations.b: The missing coupon does not mean a missing return. The bill is bought $300 below face, and that pull from $9,700 to $10,000 is the dollar return.
distractorExplanations.c: The $9,700 purchase price is the cash invested, not profit, and it is not paid again on top of face value. Profit is $10,000 minus $9,700, which is $300.
distractorExplanations.d: Receiving $10,000 returns the $9,700 of cash invested plus $300 of discount. Counting the whole face amount as profit ignores the price the investor paid.

prompt: An ETF's intraday indicative value is $50. During the session its shares trade at $50.75. An investor who buys one share on the exchange pays:

options.text: $50.00, because ETF shares are purchased at indicative value
$50.75, the live market price, which is $0.75 above indicative value
$49.25, the $50 indicative value minus the $0.75 gap
$50.00 at the close, because the $50.75 intraday print is not a real trade

explanation: ETF shares trade on an exchange throughout the day at market prices that can differ from the indicative value. A buyer who pays the $50.75 market price pays $50.75, which is $0.75 above the $50 indicative value. Creation and redemption can pull that gap back toward zero, but this purchase prints at the market price.

distractorExplanations.a: Indicative value is a reference for the underlying basket, not the price of every exchange trade. This share is trading at $50.75, and that is the price the buyer pays.
distractorExplanations.c: Subtracting the $0.75 gap from $50 would be a discount. The shares are trading above the $50 indicative value, so the buyer pays $50.75, not $49.25.
distractorExplanations.d: A once-a-day price at the close describes an open-end mutual fund. This ETF trade happens during the session and is filled at the $50.75 market price.

prompt: A 40-year-old client compares a 20-year term policy with a $500,000 death benefit and no cash value to a variable life policy with the same $500,000 death benefit and a cash value invested in subaccounts. The policy that builds a cash value the owner can access is:

options.text: The term policy, because its $500,000 death benefit is cash the owner can take while alive
Neither policy, because both pay $500,000 and neither one builds a cash value
The term policy, because the lack of a cash value turns the term premium into a savings balance
The variable life policy, because its cash value is invested in subaccounts the owner selects

explanation: Term insurance pays a death benefit for a stated period, here 20 years, and this policy builds no cash value, so it is protection rather than an investment balance. Variable life keeps a cash value invested in subaccounts the owner chooses, and that cash value is the amount the owner can access. Both policies list a $500,000 death benefit; only the variable life policy accumulates an investment value.

distractorExplanations.a: The $500,000 term benefit is paid if the insured dies during the 20-year term. It is not a balance the owner can withdraw while alive, because this term policy has no cash value.
distractorExplanations.b: The death benefits match at $500,000, but the cash-value designs do not. Variable life invests a cash value in subaccounts; this term policy has no cash value at all.
distractorExplanations.c: A term premium on a policy with no cash value pays for insurance over the 20-year term. It is not deposited into a savings balance the owner can access.

prompt: Under the Investment Advisers Act, a fiduciary adviser must

options.text: Put the client's interests ahead of their own
Avoid written disclosures
Maximize firm revenue regardless of client impact
Only follow suitability, never loyalty

explanation: A fiduciary adviser owes loyalty and care. Loyalty puts the client's interest ahead of the adviser's revenue, and care requires a reasonable inquiry plus full disclosure of material conflicts. Suitability alone, or skipping disclosure, does not meet that standard.

distractorExplanations.b: Avoiding written disclosure hides conflicts. Fiduciary care requires disclosing material conflicts, not omitting them.
distractorExplanations.c: Maximizing firm revenue regardless of the client puts the adviser first and breaches the duty of loyalty.
distractorExplanations.d: A suitability check is a lower standard. An adviser's fiduciary duty adds loyalty and care on top of suitability.

prompt: Asset allocation's primary purpose is to:

options.text: Spread risk across asset classes in line with goals and risk tolerance
Pick the individual securities expected to outperform within each sector
Shift between stocks and cash based on short-term market forecasts
Maximize expected return by concentrating in the best-performing asset class

explanation: Asset allocation divides a portfolio among asset classes such as stocks, bonds, and cash so the overall mix of risk and expected return fits the client's goals, time horizon, and risk tolerance; it drives most long-run variability in portfolio returns.

distractorExplanations.b: Choosing individual winners is security selection, a separate step from allocating among asset classes.
distractorExplanations.c: Forecast-driven switching is market timing, not the purpose of strategic asset allocation.
distractorExplanations.d: Concentrating in one class abandons diversification; allocation balances risk and return to goals.

prompt: A 28-year-old with a long horizon and high risk tolerance is often suited to:

options.text: A higher bond allocation than a retiree who needs portfolio income soon
A higher equity allocation than a retiree needing income soon
Heavy use of margin to boost equity exposure beyond 100%
A stable-value and money-market core to avoid volatility

explanation: A long horizon gives time to recover from equity declines, so a higher stock weight than a retiree who must spend soon is often suitable when the client can also stand the volatility. That is not a mandate to borrow on margin or to hold only cash.

distractorExplanations.a: Reverses the logic; a long horizon and high tolerance support more equities, not more bonds.
distractorExplanations.c: High risk tolerance does not make leverage the default; margin adds risk beyond a suitable baseline.
distractorExplanations.d: A cash-like core suits short horizons; over decades it exposes a young investor to inflation erosion.

prompt: Tax-efficient placement often suggests holding

options.text: Tax-inefficient assets in tax-advantaged accounts when appropriate
Never using asset location
All munis inside a traditional IRA for maximum benefit
High-turnover taxable bond funds in taxable accounts and ignoring IRAs

explanation: Tax-aware asset location places holdings that generate ordinary income or frequent gains in tax-advantaged accounts when that improves after-tax wealth, without changing the household's overall mix. Municipal bonds are the usual exception, because their exemption works in a taxable account.

distractorExplanations.b: Refusing to consider which account holds an asset gives up a tax benefit that does not require a different risk mix.
distractorExplanations.c: Municipal interest is already tax-exempt, so placing those bonds in a traditional IRA wastes the exemption and taxes later withdrawals.
distractorExplanations.d: High-turnover taxable bond funds throw off income that a tax-advantaged account could shelter; leaving them taxable reverses the usual placement.

prompt: Required minimum distributions (RMDs) generally apply to:

options.text: Roth IRAs during the original owner's lifetime
Taxable brokerage accounts once the account owner reaches age 73
Traditional IRAs/401(k)s after the applicable RMD age
529 plans once the beneficiary reaches age 18

explanation: Required minimum distributions force withdrawals from pre-tax accounts such as traditional IRAs and 401(k)s once the owner reaches the statutory age. A Roth IRA has no lifetime required distribution for the original owner, a taxable brokerage account has none, and a 529 plan is not a retirement account. Congress has moved that age in the SECURE Acts, so the rule is the applicable age rather than one fixed birthday.

distractorExplanations.a: Roth IRAs have no RMDs while the original owner is alive; RMDs target pre-tax accounts.
distractorExplanations.b: RMDs apply to tax-deferred retirement accounts; taxable brokerage accounts have no required distributions.
distractorExplanations.d: 529 plans have no federal required distribution at 18; assets can stay invested for later education costs.

A target return the adviser commits to achieving each year
Short-term market forecasts that drive monthly allocation shifts
Goals, constraints, risk tolerance, and allocation guidelines

prompt: Which statement best describes dollar-cost averaging?

options.text: Avoiding equities entirely
Buying only at market bottoms with perfect foresight
A type of municipal pre-refunding
Investing a fixed dollar amount at regular intervals

explanation: Dollar-cost averaging invests a fixed dollar amount on a set schedule, so the client buys more shares when prices are lower and fewer when prices are higher. It does not require calling market bottoms, and it is neither a ban on equities nor a municipal refinancing technique.

distractorExplanations.a: Avoiding equities is an allocation choice. Dollar-cost averaging is a purchase schedule, and it is often used to buy stocks.
distractorExplanations.b: Buying only at bottoms would require forecasting the low. Dollar-cost averaging invests on schedule without that forecast.

prompt: A client needing funds in 12 months for a house down payment should prioritize

options.text: Growth stocks to build the down payment faster
Long-term bonds to lock in higher current yields
A balanced 60/40 portfolio to blend growth with steady income
Capital preservation and liquidity over high expected return

explanation: A down payment due in about twelve months has a short horizon, so principal and access come before expected return. Growth stocks, long-term bonds, and a balanced mix can all fall before the purchase and leave the client short of cash.

distractorExplanations.a: A 12-month goal cannot absorb an equity drawdown; growth stocks risk a shortfall when cash is needed.

prompt: Modern portfolio theory emphasizes that diversification can

options.text: Remove systematic risk by combining many assets across sectors
Reduce systematic risk by combining perfectly correlated assets
Raise expected return above the highest-returning asset held
Reduce unsystematic risk by combining imperfectly correlated assets

explanation: Combining assets that do not move perfectly together cancels some security-specific risk. Market risk remains, because it is shared across assets and is not removed by holding more names. Expected return stays a weighted average; it does not rise above the best asset held.

distractorExplanations.a: Systematic (market) risk remains however many assets are held; diversification reduces unsystematic risk.
distractorExplanations.b: Perfectly correlated assets give no diversification benefit, and it is unsystematic risk that falls.
distractorExplanations.c: A portfolio's expected return is a weighted average; diversification improves risk, not return beyond the best asset.

prompt: When assessing risk tolerance, an adviser should consider:

Only the client's age by a rigid formula
Only the adviser's favorite sector

explanation: A suitable risk level joins the client's willingness to endure declines with the financial ability to absorb them, plus goals, liquidity, taxes, and time horizon. Age is one input, and the adviser's favorite sector is not a substitute for that profile.

distractorExplanations.b: Liquidity needs can force a sale at a bad time, so ignoring them overstates how much market risk the client can take.

prompt: In individual income taxation, a progressive tax system means:

options.text: Marginal rates rise as taxable income rises
Everyone pays the same percentage of income
Lower earners pay a higher share of income
Tax rates rise as the holding period of assets lengthens

explanation: In a progressive system the marginal rate on the next dollar of taxable income rises as income moves into higher brackets. That is different from a flat percent of all income, from a regressive burden, and from the holding-period rule for capital gains.

Sells winners and buys laggards to restore targets

prompt: Behavioral bias: loss aversion means investors often

Anchor on the price they originally paid for a stock
Feel losses more strongly than equivalent gains
Follow the crowd into popular investments

prompt: For a tax-sensitive taxable account, which is often more tax-efficient?

options.text: Ignoring wash-sale rules while day-trading the same security
Frequent short-term gain harvesting for fun
High-turnover active trading each week
Low-turnover index equity exposure

explanation: In a taxable account, low-turnover index equity realizes fewer gains and more often qualifies those gains for long-term treatment. Weekly trading, intentional short-term gains, and wash-sale violations each create tax the client was trying to avoid.

distractorExplanations.a: The wash-sale rule disallows a loss when a substantially identical security is bought again too soon. It is not a license to day-trade the same security.
distractorExplanations.b: Realizing short-term gains on purpose accelerates tax, often at ordinary rates, which works against a tax-sensitive taxable account.
distractorExplanations.c: High weekly turnover creates repeated taxable events and short-term gains, the drag a tax-sensitive account is trying to reduce.

prompt: ERISA fiduciary standards (for plan fiduciaries) emphasize

options.text: Acting solely in the interest of plan participants/beneficiaries
Ignoring diversification
Maximizing revenue-sharing without disclosure
Selecting the highest-cost share class deliberately without analysis

explanation: ERISA requires a plan fiduciary to act solely in the interest of participants and beneficiaries, with the care of a prudent expert, and to diversify plan investments. Undisclosed revenue sharing, ignored diversification, and an unjustified high-cost share class each fail that duty.

distractorExplanations.b: ERISA requires diversification of plan assets so one holding does not dominate the risk borne by participants.
distractorExplanations.c: Taking revenue sharing without disclosure puts the fiduciary's compensation ahead of participants and breaches loyalty.
distractorExplanations.d: Picking the highest-cost share class on purpose, with no analysis, fails the duty of prudence owed to participants.
